name: Scepticism's tolerant, hostile-to-religion character and Sextus Empiricus's case against theism
plain_explanation: Later Sceptics went along with ordinary religious rituals as a matter of custom while refusing to actually believe the underlying doctrines, and some, like Sextus Empiricus, wrote direct arguments that believing in a providential god leads either to blaming God for evil or admitting God is weak or uncaring.
precise_definition: The distinction, illustrated by Sextus Empiricus's surviving treatise, between practical conformity to religious custom and intellectual assent to religious belief, together with an early version of the problem of evil used as an argument against dogmatic theism.
why_it_mattered: Shows Scepticism functioning as a mainly negative, corrosive force against dogmatic religion in antiquity, without the positive scientific alternative that later, modern scepticism would pair with.
historical_origin: Late ancient Scepticism, transmitted through Sextus Empiricus (second-third century A.D.), possibly drawing on Carneades via Clitomachus.
examples: 'If they say that God controls everything, they make Him the author of evil things; if... He controls some things only, or nothing, they are compelled to make God either grudging or impotent'
connection_to_politics_or_religion: Directly targets dogmatic theism, while endorsing outward conformity to state religious practice.
